quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [have never buy] anything from that online shop before now.
quests.hint: 'Buy' has an irregular past participle used with 'have' in the present perfect.
quests.explanation: The present perfect needs the past participle, and 'buy' irregularly becomes 'bought': 'have never bought.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [Have you ever return] a gift that you knew someone would notice?
quests.hint: Present perfect questions with 'ever' still need the past participle form of the verb.
quests.explanation: 'Return' is a regular verb, so its past participle is 'returned': 'Have you ever returned.' The base form alone doesn't fit the present perfect structure.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She [has already try on] three different dresses at the boutique today.
quests.hint: The main verb needs its past participle form to complete the present perfect structure.
quests.explanation: 'Try' becomes 'tried' as its past participle, so the correct present perfect form is 'has already tried on.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [have never tasting] food this spicy in my entire life!
quests.hint: The verb form after 'have' in the present perfect must be the past participle, not '-ing.'
quests.explanation: Present perfect requires 'have/has + past participle.' The correct form is 'have never tasted,' not the '-ing' form.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [Has your brother ever cook] a full meal completely on his own?
quests.hint: Present perfect questions place 'has' before the subject, followed by the past participle.
quests.explanation: The structure needs the past participle after 'has': 'Has your brother ever cooked.' The base form 'cook' alone is incomplete here.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We [have already eat], so we don't need a table right now.
quests.hint: 'Eat' has an irregular past participle, different from its simple past form.
quests.explanation: 'Eat' becomes 'eaten' as its past participle (not 'ate,' which is the simple past), so 'have already eaten' is correct.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [have lost] my phone yesterday, so I need to buy a new one.
quests.hint: The word 'yesterday' is a specific past time marker — which tense pairs with specific times?
quests.explanation: Specific past time expressions like 'yesterday' require the simple past, not the present perfect. The correct form is simply 'lost.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [lost] my keys somewhere, so I can't get into the apartment right now.
quests.hint: No specific time is mentioned, and the result still matters right now — which tense fits that?
quests.explanation: Without a specific past time, and with a present result (being locked out now), the present perfect 'have lost' is the better fit.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She [repaired] her laptop three times since she bought it last year.
quests.hint: The phrase 'since... last year' points to an ongoing period leading up to now.
quests.explanation: 'Since' signals an unfinished time period continuing to the present, which requires the present perfect: 'has repaired.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [have seen] the doctor last Tuesday for a routine check-up.
quests.hint: 'Last Tuesday' is a specific, finished point in the past.
quests.explanation: Because 'last Tuesday' is a specific completed time, the simple past 'saw' is correct rather than the present perfect.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [never took] this particular medicine before, so I'm a little cautious.
quests.hint: No specific past time is mentioned, and the relevance continues into the present.
quests.explanation: Without a specific time reference, and with present relevance, 'have never taken' (present perfect) fits better than the simple past.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: He [went] to the gym three times this week already, which is impressive.
quests.hint: 'This week' is an unfinished time period that includes the present moment.
quests.explanation: Because 'this week' is a time period still in progress, the present perfect 'has gone' is correct rather than the simple past.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: You [have to] buy a ticket in advance; you can simply pay at the door.
quests.hint: The second half of the sentence describes an easy alternative — does that suggest a requirement or its absence?
quests.explanation: Since paying at the door is presented as an easy alternative, there's no requirement to book in advance, so 'don't have to' is correct.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We [don't have to] arrive early if we want the best seats at the concert.
quests.hint: Getting good seats usually depends on arriving before others, which implies a requirement.
quests.explanation: Because arriving early is necessary for good seats, the sentence needs 'have to,' expressing obligation, not its absence.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She [have to] finish her project before she can watch the new series.
quests.hint: Focus on subject-verb agreement — 'she' requires the third-person singular form.
quests.explanation: 'She' is a singular subject, so 'have to' must become 'has to' to agree correctly.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: You [have to] shout — I can hear you perfectly well from here.
quests.hint: The statement that the listener can already hear fine suggests no requirement to shout.
quests.explanation: Since the speaker can already hear clearly, there's no need to shout, so 'don't have to' correctly expresses the absence of obligation.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We [don't have to] reply to this email by Friday, as the request states.
quests.hint: A stated deadline in the sentence usually implies an actual requirement.
quests.explanation: Because the sentence describes a stated request with a deadline, 'have to' correctly expresses the obligation to reply.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: He [have to] explain everything again because no one understood the first time.
quests.hint: Check subject-verb agreement for the singular subject 'he.'
quests.explanation: Since 'he' is singular, the verb must be 'has to,' not the base form 'have to,' to maintain correct agreement.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The neighbor [which] waters our plants always leaves a friendly note.
quests.hint: The relative pronoun refers to a person, not a thing.
quests.explanation: 'Who' is used for people, while 'which' refers to things or animals. Since 'neighbor' is a person, 'who' is correct.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The app [who] I use every morning tracks my sleep and daily steps.
quests.hint: The relative pronoun here refers to a thing, not a person.
quests.explanation: 'Which' refers to things, such as an app, while 'who' is reserved for people. The correct pronoun here is 'which.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: That's the family [who's] dog barks every night in our neighborhood.
quests.hint: This sentence expresses possession — the dog belongs to the family.
quests.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession ('the family's dog'), while 'who's' is simply a contraction of 'who is.' The context calls for the possessive form.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The teacher [which] taught me chemistry last year just retired from the school.
quests.hint: The relative pronoun refers to a person — the teacher.
quests.explanation: Since 'teacher' refers to a person, the correct relative pronoun is 'who,' not 'which,' which is used for things.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The textbook [who] we use in class is quite outdated by now.
quests.hint: The relative pronoun refers to a thing — a textbook.
quests.explanation: 'Which' is the correct relative pronoun for things like a textbook; 'who' is reserved for people.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: That's the student [who's] backpack was left in the classroom yesterday.
quests.hint: This sentence expresses possession — the backpack belongs to the student.
quests.explanation: 'Whose' correctly shows ownership of the backpack, while 'who's' is only a contraction for 'who is,' which doesn't fit here.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If I [will finish] the report on time, my manager will be very pleased.
quests.hint: In the first conditional, the 'if' clause uses the present tense, not 'will.'
quests.explanation: First conditional sentences use present tense in the 'if' clause and 'will' only in the result clause. The correct form is simply 'finish.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If you send the email now, the client [receives] it before the meeting starts.
quests.hint: The result clause of a first conditional uses 'will' plus the base verb.
quests.explanation: The result clause needs 'will + base verb': 'will receive.' Using the present tense here breaks the standard first-conditional pattern.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If we [will have] enough time, we'll review the entire budget again tomorrow.
quests.hint: The 'if' clause of a first conditional stays in the present tense.
quests.explanation: 'Will' does not belong in the 'if' clause of a first conditional; the correct form is the simple present, 'have.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If the weather [will be] nice tomorrow, we'll go hiking in the mountains.
quests.hint: Keep the 'if' clause in the present tense, even though the sentence refers to the future.
quests.explanation: The 'if' clause of a first conditional always uses the present tense, so 'is' is correct rather than 'will be.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If we miss this flight, we [have] to wait six hours for the next one.
quests.hint: The main clause describing the future result needs 'will' plus the base verb.
quests.explanation: The result clause requires 'will + base verb': 'will have to wait.' The plain present tense doesn't fit the future result here.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: If you [will forget] your passport at home, you won't be able to board.
quests.hint: The condition clause should remain in the simple present tense.
quests.explanation: 'Will' is not used in the 'if' clause of a first conditional; the simple present 'forget' is the correct form.
